tip: The imperfect plus 'da' plus a time span means had been doing: 'cercavi da tempo' = you had been looking for a while.
'Fare' has the irregular past participle 'fatto', so the perfect tense is 'hai fatto', not 'hai fato'.
Object pronouns attach to an infinitive, which drops its final '-e': 'dire' plus 'ti' becomes 'dirti'.
'Ci sono' means there are (plural); 'c'è' means there is (singular). Many tourists takes 'ci sono': 'ci sono molti turisti'.
'Bello' shortens to 'bel' before many masculine singular nouns: 'bel tramonto'.
'Dei', from 'di' plus 'i', means some before most masculine plural nouns: 'dei fiori'.
'Simpatico' means nice or likeable, not sympathetic.
Italian keeps both negatives: 'non' before the verb plus 'nessuno' after it together mean not anyone: 'non conoscevo nessuno'.
The article with a weekday means every one of them: 'il lunedì' = on Mondays.
The imperfect sets the background, the perfect marks the event: 'nevicava' (was snowing) frames 'abbiamo chiuso' (we closed).
For health and how you feel, use 'stare', not 'essere': 'sto bene' = I'm well, literally I stay well.
Italian often uses 'avere' (have) where English uses be: 'ha torto' = he's wrong, literally he has wrong.
Fear takes 'avere', not 'essere': 'ha paura' = she's afraid, literally she has fear.
Put 'più' before an adjective or adverb to say more: 'più forte' = louder.
Names of languages usually take the definite article: 'studi l'italiano' = you study Italian.
'Bene' is the adverb (well); 'buono' is the adjective (good): 'canta bene' = sings well.
The present tense also covers the near future: 'parte stasera' = he's leaving tonight.
Use 'stare' plus an adjective for a temporary state: 'sta zitto' = he keeps quiet.
'Parere' means to seem, an everyday match for 'sembrare': 'pare contento' = he seems happy.
Unlike English, nationalities are written in lowercase: 'sono italiano' = I am Italian.
'È' with an accent is the verb is; 'e' without it means and: 'lui è alto' = he is tall.
Adjectives ending in '-e' use one plural, '-i', for both genders: 'felici'.
Adjectives ending in '-e' like 'triste' do not change for gender: a man or a woman is equally 'triste'.
Questions normally keep statement word order; only the rising tone changes: 'sei sicuro?'
Being right takes 'avere': 'avere ragione' = to be right, literally to have reason.
To make a verb negative, place 'non' before it: 'non ho capito' = I didn't understand.
For an informal '-are' command, drop '-re' and end in '-a': 'mangia' = eat.
Informal commands from '-ere' and '-ire' verbs end in '-i': 'chiudi' = close.
Being in a hurry uses 'avere': 'abbiamo fretta' = we're in a hurry, literally we have hurry.
Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel, 'una' drops its 'a': 'un'applicazione'.
